notes: Guess community strings (public/private/manager) with onesixtyone, then walk with snmpwalk/snmpbulkwalk. v1/v2c are cleartext — dump processes, routes, ARP, running config, and sometimes credentials. Key Windows OIDs: users (1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25), processes (1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2), installed software (1.3.6.1.2.1.25.6.3.1.2), open TCP ports (1.3.6.1.2.1.6.13.1.3). Check the extended MIB (NET-SNMP-EXTEND) for command output. OSCP workflow: (1) nmap -sU --open -p 161 <cidr> to find hosts, (2) onesixtyone to brute community strings, (3) snmpwalk to dump data. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 6 (Information Gathering). Build a community wordlist from common defaults (public, private, manager) and sweep with onesixtyone before full snmpwalk. Use -v1 with -t 10 for slow targets. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 6.

recommended.note: Brute any service creds discovered in the MIB.

defense.why_it_works: SNMPv1 'has no built-in authentication mechanism, meaning anyone accessing the network can read and modify network data' and 'does not support encryption, meaning that all data is sent in plain text.' SNMPv2c community strings 'are only transmitted in plain text' over the network, allowing interception. Many organizations remain on SNMPv2 because 'the transition to SNMPv3 can be very complex.' Dangerous misconfigurations include: rwuser noauth (full OID tree access without any authentication) and rwcommunity (write access regardless of source IP).
defense.prerequisites: Network access to SNMP (UDP 161) and a valid community string (often the default 'public').
defense.impact: System, process, interface, and software details from the MIB — sometimes including credentials.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for execution of network enumeration utilities (nmap, netcat, net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, particularly when chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands. [AN1584] Sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands issued from bash scripts or interactive shells to map remote hosts are a strong behavioral indicator.
defense.artifacts: SNMP GET/WALK requests to UDP 161 in network logs; agent access logs where enabled.
defense.prevention:
Upgrade to SNMPv3, which adds username/password authentication and pre-shared key encryption. Remove rwuser noauth and rwcommunity entries from snmpd.conf. Restrict SNMP access to specific management IPs via firewall rules on UDP 161/162. Change default community strings from 'public'/'private'.

[MITRE T1046 M1042] Disable or remove unnecessary services and functionality that expose attack surface. [M1030] Implement network segmentation to limit the set of hosts reachable from any given compromised system. Use firewalls to restrict which source addresses can reach each service port.
defense.evasion: Query specific OIDs rather than walking the entire MIB to cut request volume, and use the correct community string so the traffic looks like legitimate management polling; space requests out to avoid rate-based alerts.
defense.misconfiguration: SNMP v1/v2c uses community strings (essentially cleartext passwords) for authentication. The default community string 'public' grants read access on many devices and is almost never changed. SNMPv3 with authentication+encryption is available but rarely deployed. SNMP exposes system information: OS version, running processes, network interfaces, installed software, routing tables — all useful for reconnaissance.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# snmpd.conf (Linux) — default public community with overly broad access:
rocommunity public default
# 'public' = world-readable SNMP, 'default' = from any source IP
# Also: rwcommunity private  <-- write access with trivially guessed string

# Windows SNMP service — default community 'public' with read permissions:
# HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SNMP\Parameters\ValidCommunities
#   public = 4  (READ ONLY, but accessible to any host)
defense.secure_config:
# Option 1 — Disable SNMP entirely (if not needed):
systemctl stop snmpd && systemctl disable snmpd
# Windows: Stop-Service SNMP; Set-Service SNMP -StartupType Disabled

# Option 2 — Upgrade to SNMPv3 with auth+encryption:
# /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf:
createUser monuser SHA 'SecureAuthPass2024!' AES 'SecurePrivPass2024!'
rouser monuser authPriv .1.3.6    # read-only, auth+priv required

# Remove v1/v2c community access:
#   Comment out or delete all rocommunity/rwcommunity lines

# Firewall — restrict SNMP (UDP/161) to monitoring hosts only:
iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 161 -s 10.10.1.20 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 161 -j DROP
